extracted.intended_audience: writers and readers interested in representing New England (Yankee) dialect and character in 19th-century poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for representing the New England (Yankee) dialect and character in metrical and prose writing, including pronunciation-to-spelling rules, authenticity of provincialisms, and how to avoid caricature. Intended to guide spelling choices in verse and the depiction of Yankee character traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle: adapt spelling to ordinary pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the metrical portion of the book, I have endeavored to adapt the spelling as nearly as possible to the ordinary mode of pronunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorially: adjust orthography in verse to reflect how words are actually pronounced by speakers of the dialect; this is a deliberate choice to render speech authentically in metrical lines. Caveat to readers: the author has been 'over-particular' and offers a classical caution (Martial) if objected to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of provincialisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader will not find one [provincialisms] which is not (as I believe) either native or imported with the early settlers, nor one which I have not, with my own ears, heard in familiar use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only provincialisms that are historically or locally attested (native or imported by settlers) and preferably those personally verified by the writer; avoid inventing unmoored archaisms presented as authentic. The author defends choices on grounds of attested usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to coin new words as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Undoubtedly, we have a right to make new words, as they are needed by the fresh aspects under which life presents itself here in the New World; and, indeed, wherever a language is alive, it grows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When novel experiences or local realities require new vocabulary, neologisms are acceptable; but this sits alongside the preference for historically grounded provincialisms. New coinages should serve expressive need, not mere novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1: r pronunciation (drop or avoid the 'rough' r)
rubrics_metrics.description: The genuine Yankee never gives the rough sound to the r when he can help it, and often displays considerable ingenuity in avoiding it even before a vowel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In representing speech, omit or soften the rhotic 'r' where appropriate (non-rhotic pronunciation), including before vowels; use spelling choices that reflect that avoidance rather than forcing an r-sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 2: final g and d often dropped
rubrics_metrics.description: He seldom sounds the final g, a piece of self-denial, if we consider his partiality for nasals. The same of the final d, as han' and stan' for hand and stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render participles and -ed/-ing/-and endings with dropped final consonants where the dialect omits them (e.g., 'han'' for 'hand', 'stan'' for 'stand'); show examples in orthography to reflect pronunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 3: h-dropping in while/when/where
rubrics_metrics.description: The h in such words as while, when, where, he omits altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When transcribing spoken dialect, omit initial 'h' in these words (e.g., 'while' -> 'wile'/'hile' depending on chosen scheme) to match observed pronunciation; be consistent in usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 4: variability of the vowel 'a'
rubrics_metrics.description: In regard to a, he shows some inconsistency, sometimes giving a close and obscure sound, as hev for have, hendy for handy, ez for as, thet for that, and again giving it the broad sound it has in father, as hânsome for handsome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent the vowel 'a' flexibly: sometimes render it as reduced/close (hev, ez, thet), other times as broad (hânsome). Choose forms that match the word's spoken realization in context rather than applying a single rule to all 'a's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 5: an 'e' prefix before the 'ou' sound and recitation model
rubrics_metrics.description: To the sound ou he prefixes an e (hard to exemplify otherwise than orally). The following passage in Shakespeare he would recite thus: [dialect-rendered Shakespeare passage].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing sounds spelled 'ou' (as in 'now', 'out'), consider an initial 'e' to indicate the dialectal quality (e.g., 'neow' for 'now'); consult the provided recited Shakespeare passage as an explicit orthographic model demonstrating multiple combined substitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 6: au pronounced 'ah' (daughter, slaughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Au, in such words as daughter and slaughter, he pronounces ah.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render 'daughter'/'slaughter' with an 'ah' vowel in spelling (e.g., 'dahter'/'slahter' or similar), to reflect the dialectal pronunciation choice; be consistent with chosen orthography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 7: add a drawl 'ad libitum'
rubrics_metrics.description: To the dish thus seasoned add a drawl ad libitum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond the described phonological substitutions, freely add a lengthening/drawl where appropriate for character and rhythm; this is discretionary and should be used to enhance authenticity and effect, not gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict Yankee character with nuance, not angular caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Yankee character has wanted neither open maligners, nor even more dangerous enemies in the persons of those unskilful painters who have given to it that hardness, angularity, and want of proper perspective, which, in truth, belonged, not to their subject, but to their own niggard and unskilful pencil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one-dimensional, harsh caricatures. Instead portray the Yankee as a complex product of history and environment: thrifty, inventive, practical ('mystic-practicalism'), longanimous, 'good at patching', 'not so careful for what is best as for what will do', 'armed at all points against Hunger', etc. Use these listed traits as positive descriptive touchstones rather than flattening stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual/historical justification for dialect choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Any one much read in the writings of the early colonists need not be told that the far greater share of the words and phrases now esteemed peculiar to New England, and local there, were brought from the mother country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or choosing archaisms and provincialisms, situate them historically: many so-called peculiar words are heritage items from early colonists or King James-era usages. Use historical sources and contemporary oral attestations to justify dialectal vocabulary and forms.
